What did SyncGap-v1 show for segments with three distinctive, time-spread anchors under stationary, known-median delays?

In SyncGap-v1, 42% of those segments retained at least 95% of their prior drift-interval width. In those segments, the reported drift interval narrowed by no more than 5% relative to its prior width; it may have narrowed less. The 42% applies specifically to segments meeting all the conditions you named, not to every segment in SyncGap-v1.
Can you unpack ‘retained at least 95% of prior drift-interval width’?

It compares the reported drift interval with its prior interval. If the prior interval has some width, retaining at least 95% means the reported interval remains at least 0.95 times as wide. It is a statement about how little the interval contracted, not a claim that the clock drift itself is 95% of some value.
And 42% is the share with that small amount of contraction?

Yes. The reported share is 42% of the SyncGap-v1 segments that had three distinctive, time-spread anchors and stationary, known-median delays. For that share, the resulting drift-interval width was at least 95% of the prior width. The evidence does not give the corresponding widths for the other 58%.
Do we know whether every interval in that 42% narrowed a little?

No. ‘At least 95% of prior width’ includes an interval that narrowed by up to 5%, one that did not narrow, and potentially one that became wider. The stated result supplies a lower bound on retained width, not an exact width or direction of change for each segment.
Does the finding concern clock-offset error as well as drift uncertainty?

The reported finding concerns drift-interval width. It does not report clock-offset estimation errors, so it cannot establish an error comparison with global-offset alignment or whether the 25% median clock-offset error-reduction target was achieved.
What does it tell us about the information supplied by three anchors?

For the reported 42%, even three anchors described as distinctive and time-spread, together with stationary, known-median delays, were associated with little contraction of the drift interval relative to its prior width. The observation matters because anchor count, distinctiveness, and spread do not by themselves tell us how much the resulting interval will narrow in every segment. It does not specify what happened in each remaining segment.
Should I interpret ‘distinctive’ as saying there was no possible matching uncertainty?

No such absolute claim is stated. ‘Distinctive’ characterizes the anchors in the reported condition, but the result does not provide a separate measure of correspondence certainty. Nor does it identify which source of uncertainty accounts for the retained interval width.
Could drifting event delays explain the wide intervals in this particular group?

The reported group is specifically under stationary, known-median delays, so it should not be described as the drifting-delay condition. The evidence also does not identify a cause for the limited interval contraction. It establishes the interval-width observation under the stated condition, without attributing it to a particular mechanism.
Does a known median imply that each anchor had a known event delay?

No. A known median is a reference for event delays; it does not specify the delay of every individual event. The reported result should retain that distinction: it occurred under stationary, known-median delays, not under a claim that all three event delays were individually known.
Does retaining nearly all the prior width prove the clock drift was not identifiable from the observed modalities?

It shows limited narrowing by the reported drift interval for those segments. On its own, the width comparison does not prove a particular formal identifiability conclusion: it does not supply the interval construction, the observations for each segment, or a comparison of alternative timing explanations. It is appropriate to report the persistent uncertainty without claiming a more specific identifiability result than the evidence states.
Could the reported intervals be multimodal because of periodic repeats?

This finding does not say whether these segments contained periodic repeats or whether their posteriors had multiple modes. Retained interval width and multimodality are different properties. We should not infer a repeat-driven explanation from the width statistic alone.
Does the 95% figure say anything about ambiguity coverage?

Not directly. Here, 95% is a fraction of prior drift-interval width, not a posterior probability level or a measured coverage rate. An interval can stay wide without thereby demonstrating that it covers all relevant timing alternatives. The finding reports width retention, not ambiguity-coverage performance.
Can we tell how many segments this represents?

No count is given. We know the percentage—42% of segments satisfying the stated three-anchor and delay conditions—but not the size of that group. Converting the percentage to a number of segments would require information that is not provided.
What about omission rates? Can I say this happened at 40% omissions?

No. The finding does not assign the 42% to a particular omission rate. SyncGap-v1 included an omission sweep, but this reported result specifies the anchor and delay conditions, not how its segments were distributed across omission settings. It would be unsupported to attach the result to 40% omissions or to any other particular rate.
How would you state the finding without implying a cause or a result for the other segments?

‘On SyncGap-v1, 42% of segments with three distinctive, time-spread anchors under stationary, known-median event delays retained at least 95% of their prior drift-interval width.’ That states the population, conditions, and measured comparison. You can add that the drift intervals for those segments showed at most 5% contraction, while leaving causes and other outcomes unspecified.
The anchors were time-spread, so is it fair to assume the clock relationship was measured accurately across each whole segment?

No. Time spread describes where the anchors occur, not the accuracy of a drift estimate over the entire segment. The width result is particularly relevant here: in the reported 42%, the drift interval remained close to its prior width despite the specified anchor configuration. Accuracy and uncertainty across a segment would require their own evidence.
Would it be fair to call this a 42% failure rate for clock-offset estimation?

No. The 42% refers to limited contraction of drift intervals, not to a defined failure criterion for clock-offset estimates. Neither the offsets' errors nor a failure threshold is reported in this finding. Keeping the measured quantity explicit prevents the interval-width result from being mistaken for an offset-error rate.
What is the most important caution when relating this observation to audio–video timing ambiguity?

The observation is that substantial drift uncertainty remained, by the prior-width comparison, in 42% of the specified segments. It does not say which competing clock, delay, or event-matching explanations remained possible, nor whether those alternatives were covered by the reported intervals. We can flag the limited narrowing without filling in unreported causes or claiming that a specific ambiguity has been resolved.

I want to sharpen the hypothesis: with known-median event delays, three distinctive anchors spanning at least 10 minutes should constrain clock drift when timing jitter is at most 10 ms. Otherwise, flag the timing as ambiguous.

That is a testable hypothesis and a proposed ambiguity rule, not an established result. Its favorable condition combines a known-median delay assumption, three distinctive anchors, a span of ≥10 minutes, and jitter of ≤10 ms. If those conditions are not met, the proposed response is to flag ambiguity rather than present the drift as securely constrained.
Is the 10-minute requirement about the spacing between every pair of anchors?

No. ‘Three distinctive anchors spanning ≥10 minutes’ refers to the time span covered by the three anchors as a group. It does not specify a minimum separation for every pair or require them to be evenly spaced.
Why include a time-span threshold at all?

Drift concerns how the clock relationship changes over time. Anchors clustered within a short interval may offer limited leverage for distinguishing that change from an offset or event-delay variation. The hypothesis proposes ≥10 minutes as the span under which three distinctive anchors should constrain drift, provided the other stated conditions hold; it does not establish that the threshold is sufficient in every recording.
And what exactly does ≤10 ms refer to?

It is the hypothesis’s timing-jitter condition: jitter must be at most 10 milliseconds. That is not a claim that clock-offset error will be ≤10 ms, nor a target for genuine event delay. The statement does not specify a particular jitter distribution or measurement procedure, so those should not be read into it.
Suppose the three anchors span 10 minutes exactly and jitter is 10 ms exactly. Are the conditions met?

Yes. The inequalities are inclusive: a span of exactly 10 minutes meets ≥10 minutes, and jitter of exactly 10 ms meets ≤10 ms. The known-median delay assumption and the requirement for three distinctive anchors would also have to hold. Meeting all of them activates the hypothesis that drift should be constrained; it does not turn that prediction into a proven guarantee.
What if there are three anchors, but only two are distinctive?

Then the stated three-distinctive-anchor condition is not met. An indistinct anchor could allow alternative cross-modal matches, especially among repeated events. Under the proposed rule, that shortfall calls for an ambiguity flag; it does not, by itself, establish which matching or clock explanation is correct.
What if the three distinctive anchors span less than 10 minutes but have very low jitter?

The ≥10-minute span condition would still be unmet. Low jitter addresses one source of timing uncertainty, but the hypothesis also requires a sufficiently long anchor span. The proposed ‘otherwise’ rule calls for flagging ambiguity rather than assuming that low jitter compensates for a shorter span.
What if the span is longer than 10 minutes but jitter exceeds 10 ms?

That also falls outside the favorable conditions. A longer span does not erase the stated ≤10 ms jitter requirement. Flagging ambiguity in that case preserves the distinction between having time coverage and having sufficiently precise anchor timing under this hypothesis.
Does a known median mean the genuine event delay is fixed?

No. A known median supplies a reference for event delays; it does not give the exact delay of every event. Individual delays may still complicate the separation of clock drift from genuine event timing. The hypothesis says what should happen under its stated conditions, not that those conditions eliminate all possible delay variation.
Should we also silently assume the delays are stationary?

No. This hypothesis explicitly says ‘known-median delays’ but does not separately state a stationarity condition. Stationarity and a known median are different claims: knowing a median does not alone tell us whether delays change over time. If stationarity is needed for an interpretation, it would have to be stated rather than silently added to this hypothesis.
Could changing event delays still imitate drift even with three distinctive anchors across 10 minutes?

Potentially. Distinctive anchors reduce uncertainty about correspondence, and their span can inform a changing clock relationship, but those properties do not directly reveal each anchor’s genuine event delay. The prediction that drift should be constrained is conditional and should be examined with that possible confounding in mind. If the observed modalities cannot distinguish the explanations, the ambiguity should be flagged.
Does ‘otherwise flag ambiguity’ mean we must claim drift is impossible to estimate when one condition fails?

No. A flag communicates that the stated conditions for expecting constrained drift have not been met. It need not mean no estimate can be produced, and it should not be mistaken for proof that drift is formally nonidentifiable in every such instance. Any estimate can still be accompanied by uncertainty and the explicit ambiguity flag.
Conversely, does meeting all four conditions mean we can omit uncertainty intervals?

No. ‘Should constrain drift’ is a hypothesis about information gained, not permission to report an exact clock relationship. Posterior intervals can still communicate uncertainty, and any unresolved offset or drift-versus-delay ambiguity should remain visible. The conditions do not make an estimate infallible.
How do missing anchors interact with the rule?

What matters is whether three distinctive anchors are available with the required span and jitter under the known-median delay assumption. Missing anchors may prevent that condition from being met. The hypothesis does not say that a particular omission percentage always does so; the proposed flag applies when the specified conditions are absent.
And repeated anchors?

Repeated events can make it harder to tell which occurrences correspond. If the three anchors cannot be regarded as distinctive because multiple pairings remain plausible, the favorable condition is not established and ambiguity should be flagged. A repeated event elsewhere does not, by its mere presence, prove that these three anchors are indistinct.
Is the hypothesis specifically about reducing median clock-offset error by 25%?

No. It predicts that the stated anchor, span, delay, and jitter conditions should constrain drift and specifies when to flag ambiguity. It does not report clock-offset errors or demonstrate the separate 25% median clock-offset error-reduction target versus global-offset alignment under matched missing-event conditions.
Could we express the rule without making the threshold sound empirically established?

Yes: ‘We hypothesize that, with known-median event delays, three distinctive anchors spanning ≥10 minutes constrain clock drift when timing jitter is ≤10 ms; otherwise, flag timing ambiguity.’ Keeping ‘hypothesize’ and ‘should’ makes clear that the thresholds are proposed conditions, not a demonstrated universal boundary.
If all the conditions hold but the posterior still leaves widely different drift values plausible, which should take precedence: the prediction or the uncertainty?

Report the uncertainty. The conditions state when the hypothesis expects drift to be constrained; they do not override what the inference can actually distinguish. Widely different plausible drift values would need to remain visible, and an unresolved timing ambiguity should be flagged rather than suppressed to fit the hypothesis.
So ‘otherwise’ sets a conservative flagging rule, while the favorable case is still a prediction to evaluate?

Exactly. Failure to meet the specified conditions triggers the proposed ambiguity flag. Meeting them supports the hypothesis’s expectation that drift should be constrained, but it is not itself evidence that a particular audio–video alignment has separated clock drift from genuine event delays.

To evaluate the anchor-span and jitter hypothesis, let's stratify SyncGap-v1 segments that have known-median event delays and three distinctive anchors by span and jitter. Then measure drift-interval contraction and ambiguity-flag recall.

That focuses the activity on the specified SyncGap-v1 segments, then examines how the two measurements vary across anchor spans and jitter levels. Drift-interval contraction asks how much uncertainty about drift narrows. Ambiguity-flag recall asks whether cases identified as ambiguous are actually flagged. This describes an evaluation to perform, not its outcome.
Why restrict the analysis to segments with three distinctive anchors?

Holding that anchor description fixed makes span and jitter the dimensions being examined. It also directly addresses the hypothesis about three distinctive anchors. The restriction does not imply that all such segments have equally informative timing evidence or that their drift is identifiable.
Does ‘three distinctive anchors’ mean three in each segment, rather than three somewhere in the recording?

Yes. The unit being stratified is a segment with three distinctive anchors. Three anchors spread across a recording would not necessarily give each segment three anchors, so those descriptions should not be interchanged.
What does it mean to stratify by span?

It means comparing segments according to the time span covered by their three anchors. That makes it possible to examine whether drift intervals contract differently when the anchors cover more or less time. The activity does not specify particular span bins; the ≥10-minute condition belongs to the hypothesis being evaluated, not to an already reported result.
And jitter is a separate dimension, not another name for span?

Right. Span concerns how far apart in time the anchors extend as a group. Jitter concerns variability in their timing. Stratifying by both avoids treating a long anchor span as though it necessarily supplied precise timing, or low jitter as though it necessarily supplied a long span.
Should we specifically look at the ≥10-minute and ≤10 ms conditions?

Those are the span and jitter conditions in the hypothesis: three distinctive anchors spanning at least 10 minutes should constrain drift at timing jitter of at most 10 ms, given known-median delays. Examining the relevant strata would assess that prediction. The activity itself supplies no results showing whether either threshold separates more- from less-constrained cases.
If a segment spans exactly 10 minutes and has exactly 10 ms jitter, where does it fall relative to that hypothesis?

It meets both stated inequalities: ≥10 minutes includes exactly 10 minutes, and ≤10 ms includes exactly 10 ms. That classifies the segment under the proposed condition; it does not establish that its drift interval actually contracted.
How should we understand drift-interval contraction here?

It is the change in the width of an interval for clock drift as the segment's timing information is taken into account. The key measurement is how much narrower the interval becomes relative to an appropriate reference interval, if at all. The activity does not specify a calculation or report contraction values, so a particular numerical definition should be stated before interpreting a measured result.
Why measure an interval instead of just reporting a preferred drift value?

A preferred value can hide how many drift values remain plausible. Interval contraction addresses whether the anchors appreciably constrain drift under the stated assumptions. Even if an interval contracts, that alone does not show that event-delay or matching ambiguity has been fully resolved; the ambiguity flags address a different question.
Does a contracted drift interval tell us the clock-offset estimate is accurate?

Not on its own. Contraction measures a change in reported drift uncertainty; clock-offset error measures accuracy of an offset estimate against a reference. This activity calls for drift-interval contraction and ambiguity-flag recall. Neither should be presented as an unreported clock-offset error result.
What does ambiguity-flag recall ask us to count?

Conceptually, recall asks: among cases judged ambiguous under an explicit reference criterion, how many receive an ambiguity flag? To measure it, that criterion and what counts as a flag must be clear. The activity names the measurement but does not specify those definitions or give a recall value.
Are cases below 10 minutes or above 10 ms automatically the reference set of genuinely ambiguous cases?

No. The hypothesis proposes flagging ambiguity when its favorable conditions are not met, but failing a threshold does not by itself prove that the observed modalities cannot distinguish the timing explanations. Treating every such case as genuinely ambiguous by definition would make it harder to assess whether the flags reflect unresolved timing rather than merely reproduce the proposed rule.
Then could a segment meet both thresholds and still need an ambiguity flag?

Yes, if its observed audio and video still leave materially different timing explanations unresolved. Meeting the proposed span and jitter conditions is a prediction about when three distinctive anchors should constrain drift, not an exemption from flagging an ambiguity that remains visible in the inference.
Is high ambiguity-flag recall the same as having well-calibrated drift intervals?

No. Recall concerns whether ambiguous cases receive flags. Interval contraction concerns how much the reported range for drift narrows. A procedure could flag many ambiguous cases while its intervals behave differently across span and jitter strata, or report contracted intervals while missing ambiguities. The activity measures both because they capture distinct aspects of the question.
Would recall alone tell us whether we're flagging too many cases?

No. Recall focuses on ambiguous cases that were flagged; by itself, it does not say how often a flag was applied to a case that did not meet the reference ambiguity criterion. The stated activity asks for recall, so an additional claim about excessive flagging would require information not supplied here.
Does ‘known-median delays’ also tell us that event delays are stationary in these strata?

Not by itself. A known median is an assumption about a reference delay; stationarity concerns whether delay behavior changes over time. This activity specifies known-median-delay segments but does not separately state stationarity. The interpretation should not silently add that condition.
Could differences in interval contraction across the strata establish that span or jitter caused them?

The stratification can show how measured contraction varies with span and jitter in the selected SyncGap-v1 segments. The activity alone does not specify controls or results that would justify a causal claim. Its immediate purpose is to evaluate the proposed span-and-jitter condition while keeping the measurements and their limits explicit.
How should I describe the activity without implying we've already tested the thresholds?

‘Stratify SyncGap-v1 segments with known-median event delays and three distinctive anchors by anchor span and timing jitter. Measure drift-interval contraction and ambiguity-flag recall across those strata to evaluate the proposed ≥10-minute span and ≤10 ms jitter condition.’ That preserves the population, measurements, and hypothesis while leaving the outcome open.
What did the SyncGap-v1 span-and-jitter analysis find?

For segments with three anchors spanning ≥10 minutes and timing jitter of ≤10 ms, the reported prior drift intervals narrowed by 72%. Ambiguity flags detected 91% of unconstrained cases. The analysis concerned SyncGap-v1 segments with known-median event delays and three distinctive anchors; these figures report drift-interval contraction and ambiguity-flag detection, not clock-offset error.
What does ‘narrowed prior drift intervals 72%’ mean?

It means the reported contraction in drift-interval width relative to the prior interval was 72%. Put another way, the resulting width was 28% of the prior width on that reported measure. It does not mean the clock drift itself decreased by 72%, or that clock-offset estimation error decreased by 72%.
Did every qualifying segment's interval narrow by exactly 72%?

That is not specified. The finding gives a 72% narrowing for the qualifying segments but does not say whether that figure is a mean, a median, or another aggregate, nor does it give each segment's contraction. It should not be turned into an individual-segment guarantee.
Do the boundary values count? What about exactly 10 minutes and exactly 10 ms?

Yes. The inequalities are inclusive: an anchor span of exactly 10 minutes satisfies ≥10 minutes, and jitter of exactly 10 ms satisfies ≤10 ms. The reported stratum also has the stated three-anchor condition.
Is the 10 ms figure an offset-error bound?
No. It is a timing-jitter condition used to describe the segments. The finding supplies no 10 ms bound on clock-offset error and no numerical bound on genuine event delays.
How should I read the 91% figure?

It is the detection rate for ambiguity flags among cases classified as unconstrained: the flags detected 91% of those cases. It is not the proportion of all segments that were unconstrained, nor the proportion of all flagged segments that were truly unconstrained.
Does that tell us how often the flags were raised unnecessarily?

No. Detection among unconstrained cases does not give the false-positive rate or precision of the flags. Those would require information about flags on cases outside the unconstrained group, which this finding does not provide.
Do we know how ‘unconstrained’ was defined in this result?

The reported finding uses the term but does not give its operational definition or the number of unconstrained cases. We can accurately state that flags detected 91% of them, without adding an unstated threshold or treating ‘unconstrained’ as synonymous with every segment that misses a span or jitter condition.
Is ambiguity-flag detection the same thing as posterior ambiguity coverage?

Not necessarily. The 91% figure says whether unconstrained cases received flags. It does not establish that posterior intervals or modes covered every plausible offset or drift-versus-delay explanation. Flag detection and the completeness of a posterior uncertainty description are different questions.
Can I say that three anchors alone produced the 72% contraction?

That would omit important conditions. The reported contraction concerns three-anchor segments with a span of ≥10 minutes and jitter of ≤10 ms, within the stated known-median-delay, distinctive-anchor analysis. The result does not isolate the effect of anchor count alone.
What can we say about segments with shorter spans or higher jitter?

This finding gives no contraction percentage for those segments. Nor does it say that every segment outside the ≥10-minute, ≤10-ms stratum was unconstrained. The reported 72% should stay attached to its specified conditions.
Does the result prove that clock drift has been separated from changing genuine event delays in every qualifying segment?

No. Substantial drift-interval contraction is evidence about how much the reported uncertainty narrowed in that stratum, but it is not a per-segment proof that every alternative event-delay explanation was ruled out. The 91% flag-detection result also leaves some unconstrained cases undetected. Any ambiguity still unresolved from the observed modalities should remain explicit.
Does ‘known-median event delays’ mean the actual delay of each anchor was known?

No. It provides a known median for event delays, not the delay of each individual anchor. The drift inference can depend on that assumption without every genuine event delay being directly determined.
Can we attribute the interval narrowing specifically to the longer span rather than the low jitter?

Not from this combined result. It reports the outcome for segments satisfying both the ≥10-minute span and ≤10-ms jitter conditions. Separate effects of span and jitter would require separate reported comparisons; this finding supplies neither.
Does the result say whether repeated events caused any remaining ambiguity?

No. The two figures do not identify the causes of unconstrained cases or describe whether any posterior had separate modes from repeated-event matching. Repeats remain a possible source of correspondence ambiguity in the broader alignment problem, but they should not be assigned as the cause of this reported result.
What about performance against global-offset alignment?

Neither figure is a global-offset comparison. The 72% figure compares drift-interval width with its prior width; the 91% figure concerns detection of unconstrained cases. No clock-offset error for either alignment method is reported here, so the 25% median error-reduction target under matched missing-event conditions cannot be assessed from this finding.
Should the 72% and 91% be combined into one success percentage?

No. They have different denominators and describe different properties: contraction of prior drift intervals in the specified segment stratum, and detection by flags among unconstrained cases. Combining them would obscure what was measured.
What's a careful way to report both observations together?

‘On SyncGap-v1, segments with three distinctive anchors spanning ≥10 minutes and timing jitter of ≤10 ms, under known-median event delays, showed a reported 72% narrowing of prior drift intervals. Ambiguity flags detected 91% of unconstrained cases.’ That preserves the conditions and keeps interval contraction separate from flag detection without claiming an unreported offset-error improvement or universal identifiability.

Does exactly 10 minutes pass the gate?
Yes. The ≥10-minute condition includes exactly 10 minutes. Likewise, ≤10 ms includes exactly 10 ms of jitter. Both conditions must be met for the stated three-anchor gate.
If the anchors span 12 minutes but jitter is above 10 ms, what happens?

The three-anchor estimation condition is not met, because the jitter exceeds ≤10 ms. The decision then calls for checking posterior ambiguity. A longer span does not, under this rule, substitute for meeting the jitter condition.
And low jitter cannot make up for a span below 10 minutes?
Correct. The gate requires the span and jitter conditions together. If the span is below 10 minutes, the decision calls for a posterior ambiguity check even when jitter is ≤10 ms.
Does ‘check posterior ambiguity otherwise’ mean we automatically declare every case outside the gate nonidentifiable?

No. It specifies a check, not an automatic conclusion. Failing the gate means the stated conditions for proceeding with three-anchor drift estimation have not been met; the posterior check should reveal whether materially different timing explanations remain plausible. The decision does not say that every out-of-gate case is formally nonidentifiable.
Then is passing the gate a guarantee that the drift estimate is unambiguous?

No. The gate governs when to proceed with three-anchor drift estimation; it does not make the estimate exact or rule out every event-delay or matching ambiguity. If the posterior still indicates unresolved timing alternatives, they should not be concealed merely because the span and jitter conditions passed.
Why call this a gate rather than just noting that longer spans and lower jitter are helpful?

A gate makes the decision operational for three-anchor estimation: check whether the span is ≥10 minutes and jitter is ≤10 ms, and check posterior ambiguity otherwise. That is more specific than a general preference for informative anchors. It remains limited to the stated conditions; it does not specify how to estimate drift or define a numerical posterior-ambiguity threshold.
How should I interpret the 72% contraction in the rationale?

It refers to narrowing of prior drift intervals under the cited ≥10-minute and ≤10-ms three-anchor conditions. It does not mean drift decreased by 72%, or that clock-offset error fell by 72%. The decision uses that contraction as support for the gate, not as a per-segment guarantee.
Is the 42% unconstrained figure the other half of a 72-versus-42 accuracy comparison?

No. The decision cites ‘72% contraction versus 42% unconstrained,’ but interval contraction and the share described as unconstrained are not the same measurement.
